I'm not sure why I installed Debian in the first place - probably the commitment to being a fully-free operating system (or as close as one can pragmatically get to it) and being a major player which serves as a base for many of the other popular distributions out there. Even if the packaging system is not perfect, it's good enough for me to be on the testing branch, which gives me daily updates to packages while not compromising system stability - this way I can also report bugs that I find as a way of giving back to the community. Over the years I've written quite a handful of those and the maintainers are usually responsive and appreciative of the support (but not necessarily fast to reply or address the issues themselves).

In sum: it was one of my earliest picks and over 10 years as a Linux user I've had nothing but reasons to stick with it, especially after I took the leap from the stable branch to testing. It has many packages, a thriving community of maintainers, great support systems like bugs.debian.org, popcon, my hardware works out-of-the-box, aptitude is a great package manager, I have source repositories and build-dep tasks if I want to hack/compile something myself... Circa 2002 I purchased a HP ze4560us notebook from Best Buy. It had XP on it and I had no experience with it at all. In about an hour on a dial-up I had a completely trashed operating system. Later I found out that the firewall was turned off by default and I had not purchased any anti-virus yet. The find4u crap was especially horrible.

So I went back to Best Buy and saw a boxed set of SuSe 10.0 and saw in the paper that the Omaha, Nebraska Linux Users' Group was having an install fest the next Saturday. I re-formatted the hard drive and re-installed XP. I went to the install fest with the notebook, SuSe, and 2 big boxes of Krispy Kreme donuts. Those fine people made the notebook dual-boot, made certain the modem worked with Earthlink, and gave me a quick tutorial on Linux. Fantastic people. I searched the internet for what happened with XP and had no more problems after installing anti-virus software which turned on the firewall. Thanks, Micro$oft, HP and Best Buy setup techs for your stupidity.

I now am up to 13.1 openSuSe on my home-built computer and several other re-purposed units which dual-boot with XP for software with no Linux equivalents like WinADL for GM OBD-I in a '89 Isuzu Trooper. Scanner software sucks in Linux as well. But Brother supports Linux with their Laser printers which I use 2. Now when I buy hardware I check its compatibly with Linux.
